name: prefers-reduced-motion
meaning: Marks people with vestibular disorders or motion sensitivity (a health-adjacent setting). Roughly 5 to 15% enable it (estimates differ by platform).

access.persistence: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored
access.iframe: Readable from cross-origin iframes too (same values)

limits.headline: Can tell if you asked your device to cut down on animation
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the page loads.
can: Check whether reduced motion is on
Add the answer to a browser fingerprint
cannot: Tell why you chose it, though it can hint at motion sensitivity
limits.reach_label: One yes or no, no prompt

story.what_it_is: Tells a page whether you asked your device to cut down on animation.

marketing.name: prefers-reduced-motion
marketing.pitch: Google teaches sites to tone down animation for people who ask for less motion, such as those with vestibular disorders.

marketing.name: prefers-reduced-motion
marketing.pitch: Documents how a page can respect the system request for reduced animation.

story.for_you: You never see the check. If you set reduce motion, many pages stop zooming, sliding and spinning so you do not feel dizzy or sick.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to keep their sites usable by people who get motion sickness or migraines. Caring about this is also a legal and design standard. It can reveal a health need if logged.

use_cases.example: A landing page replaces big scroll animations with a simple fade when you ask for reduced motion.
A browser game turns off screen shake and fast camera spins when reduced motion is on.
A feed stops auto playing short looping videos and animated reactions.
An ad network swaps a spinning animated banner for a still one.
A store swaps a sliding carousel for a static grid.
A learning site turns off a bouncing mascot that distracts some students.
A wellness app uses calm cross fades instead of sweeping effects.

legit_uses: Respect OS theme and accessibility needs
abuse: Infer disability or setting for fingerprinting
